stimulus.text: This Westinghouse poster from February 1943 shows a woman factory worker in a blue work shirt and a red polka-dot bandana. She rolls up her sleeve and flexes her right arm against a bright yellow background. Large white letters across the top read "We Can Do It!" A small Westinghouse mark and the words "War Production Co-ordinating Committee" appear at the bottom.
stimulus.source_note: J. Howard Miller, "We Can Do It!", Westinghouse poster, February 1943, displayed in Westinghouse plants February 15-28, 1943. The words shown are the poster's own. The poster was made for Westinghouse workers; it became linked with "Rosie the Riveter" only in later years, while the wartime Rosie was a separate figure. Viewed before use; listed in the shared image pool as public domain.

source: original; stimulus from the shared image pool (J. Howard Miller poster, 1943)
stem: The poster and the wider government campaign to recruit women show which of the following about the wartime economy?

options.text: The government relied on women because factories had run out of raw materials
options.misconception: The shortage was a shortage of workers, not of raw materials.

options.text: Labor shortages forced the government to challenge older ideas about women's work
The government planned to keep women in factory jobs after the war
options.misconception: After the war women were urged to give up factory jobs to returning veterans.

options.text: Labor unions demanded that women be paid the same wages as men
options.misconception: Women in war plants were often paid less than men for the same work.

rationales.A: Factories were short of workers because men had left for the military, not because materials had run out.
rationales.B: The labor shortage was so sharp that the government urged women into industrial jobs that older custom had closed to them.
rationales.C: Background from the books: once the war ended, women workers were urged to give up their jobs so returning servicemen could take them.
rationales.D: Background from the books: women in defense plants were often paid less than men, and equal pay was not the campaign's aim.
rationales.general:
1. The poster was one piece of a government campaign to bring women into war plants.
2. Background from the books: before the war, custom discouraged women from industrial work, and the Depression had pushed women out of jobs for men.
3. With millions of men in uniform, factories could not run without new workers.
4. The government therefore set custom aside and pictured factory work as proper work for women.
Remember: when a labor shortage meets a strong custom, look for which side the government backs.
